name: lexbor
workload: Parse a ~1.5MB Google search-results HTML page 1000 times and run 5000 CSS selector queries, using Crystal/Ruby bindings for lexbor vs myhtml vs libxml2 (via the Crystagiri and Nokogiri bindings).
claimed_speedup: On AMD Ryzen 3800x: lexbor 4.75s vs libxml2/Crystagiri 14.20s parse time (~3x faster, derived from page data); CSS select 0.80s vs Nokogiri/libxml2 92.69s (~116x faster, derived from page data). On Apple M1: lexbor 2.77s vs libxml2/Crystagiri 126.25s parse time (~45x faster, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Crystal: `crystal build --release --no-debug`; Ruby 2.7 for the Nokogiri/Nokolexbor bindings
hardware: AMD Ryzen 3800x; Apple M1 (two separate benchmark runs reported)
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars on lexbor/lexbor; used by PHP's DOM/HTML extension (since PHP 8.4), Selectolax, SerpApi, Nokolexbor
tradeoffs: Pure C99, zero external dependencies, modular (HTML/CSS/URL/Encoding/Unicode). The cited benchmark measures Crystal/Ruby language bindings rather than raw C-vs-C, so results include binding/runtime overhead on both sides. A separate, independently-run benchmark for the 'fast_html' Elixir wrapper also shows lexbor beating html5ever directly (125.12ms vs html5ever's 395.21ms parsing a 6.9MB document on an AMD Ryzen 9 3950X; https://fast-html.hexdocs.pm/readme.html), though that benchmark states hardware but not exact compiler flags so it was not used as the primary citation.
caveats: The Apple M1 speedup (~45x) is far larger than the Ryzen speedup (~3x) for the identical task, suggesting the libxml2/Crystagiri build on M1 was not well optimized (e.g. no ARM-tuned path) -- treat the M1 ratio with caution rather than as a general 45x claim. Gumbo test binaries are referenced in bench/run.sh but commented out in bench/build.sh, so Gumbo numbers are not actually present in the current README despite Gumbo being a stated point of comparison.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "lexbor" "gumbo" -> found kostya/lexbor bench directory; cross-checked with gh api repos/lexbor/lexbor and repos/kostya/lexbor

name: MD4C
workload: Parse and render several Markdown files (a Pro-Git book compilation, and synthetic 1M-paragraph / 1M-emphasis / 1M-header / 1M-link files totalling ~105MB) with fresh release builds of MD4C and cmark master, measuring wall time and peak heap usage.
claimed_speedup: 1.9x-7.7x faster than cmark depending on workload (e.g. 0.0900s vs 0.4860s on many-paragraphs.md = 5.4x; 0.1100s vs 0.8460s on many-emphasis.md = 7.7x; 0.3650s vs 0.7060s on the Pro-Git benchmark input = 1.93x); ~1.8x lower peak heap on the Pro-Git input (262.74MB vs 472.13MB) and far fewer realloc() calls (36 vs 1,304,578).
compiler_and_flags: "Fresh release build of current master head for both parsers" -- exact compiler and flags not stated
hardware: 64-bit Linux machine (Slackware 14.2); specific CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 1.46k stars; bindings exist for Ruby, Lean, PHP (PECL), and Python
tradeoffs: SAX-like push parser only (no DOM), CommonMark-compliant but no built-in GFM table/strikethrough support unless the caller implements it, does no input validation by design (GIGO philosophy), assumes UTF-8 by default.
caveats: Benchmark was posted by the MD4C author himself to a CommonMark forum thread in 2017 and has not been independently reproduced since; CPU model and exact compiler flags are not stated, so despite public numbers and a described methodology it falls short of Tier A/B.

name: roxmltree
workload: Parse XML documents of four sizes (tiny/medium/large/huge) into a read-only DOM tree using `cargo bench`, comparing roxmltree against libxml2, sxd-document, and xmltree.
claimed_speedup: roxmltree faster than libxml2 across all four sizes (derived from page data): huge 2,997,887 ns vs 6,850,666 ns (~2.28x); large 1,494,886 ns vs 3,250,606 ns (~2.17x); medium 421,137 ns vs 950,984 ns (~2.26x); tiny 2,522 ns vs 8,931 ns (~3.54x).
compiler_and_flags: Rust `cargo bench` (criterion-style ns/iter output); exact rustc flags and libxml2 build flags not stated
tradeoffs: Read-only tree (no mutation or writing support), no unsafe code, no DTD support, roughly 6-8x memory overhead relative to file size; mimics lxml's parsing behavior rather than being fully spec-complete like libxml2.
caveats: Benchmark code (bench/xml.rs) is public in the repo, but the README does not state a CPU model or exact compiler/library build flags for the libxml2 comparison, so it falls short of Tier A despite being reproducible in principle; no publication date is given for the numbers.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/tafia/quick-xml/readme (pointed to RazrFalcon/roxmltree's comparison table) -> gh api repos/RazrFalcon/roxmltree/readme

name: pugixml
workload: Parse nine XML test files (1-20MB, including a 10MB XMark file and files with varying markup/content ratios) into a DOM, comparing pugixml against libxml2 (DOM and SAX modes), expat, and several other C/C++ XML parsers, on x86 and x64 builds.
claimed_speedup: On x86, pugixml faster than libxml2 (derived from raw benchmark data at benchmark-data.js): house.dae file - pugixml 0.556 us/byte vs libxml2-DOM 2.501 us/byte (~4.49x) and vs libxml2-SAX 1.500 us/byte (~2.70x); English.sml file - pugixml 0.771 us/byte vs libxml2-DOM 6.412 us/byte (~8.32x) and vs libxml2-SAX 3.218 us/byte (~4.17x).
compiler_and_flags: Microsoft Visual Studio 2015, "with all optimizations on"; exact flags not itemized
stars_or_usage: 4.65k stars; widely embedded in game engines and other C++ projects needing a lightweight XML+XPath parser
tradeoffs: In-memory DOM with compact-storage option, full XPath 1.0 support, header-light API; benchmark numbers come from a chart-rendering script (benchmark-data.js) rather than a runnable, versioned benchmark harness in the main repo, so the comparison cannot be independently re-run from the pugixml GitHub repository alone.
caveats: The pugixml.org benchmark page states hardware (Core i7 @ 2.67GHz) and compiler (MSVC 2015) but the benchmark's own source code was not found in a public repository (no pugixml-benchmark repo under the zeux GitHub account), so it falls short of Tier A despite otherwise detailed methodology. No date is given for when the benchmark was run, and the current library version (1.16) may postdate the benchmarked version.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/zeux/pugixml/readme (no numbers in README) -> WebFetch https://pugixml.org/benchmark.html and raw fetch of https://pugixml.org/benchmark-data.js for the underlying numbers
